note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. I have you down as a 68-year-old male here because of a blood test result. Tell me what happened.
Patient: My regular doctor called me two days ago. She said my PSA came back high, 6.8, and that last time it was 3.9. She said I should get it looked at, and I didn't want to wait, so I came here.
Doctor: That makes sense. When was the last one done?
Patient: About two years ago, at my yearly physical.
Doctor: Any trouble passing urine?
Patient: I get up twice a night to pee, sometimes three times, and the stream is weak. It's been that way for a year or so.
Doctor: Any burning when you urinate, or any blood in the urine?
Patient: No burning, no blood.
Doctor: Fever or chills? Any pain in your back, hips, or bones?
Patient: No fever. No bone pain either. My back is fine.
Doctor: Any weight loss that you haven't been trying for?
Patient: No, my weight has been steady.
Doctor: What medications do you take?
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg once a day for blood pressure, and atorvastatin 20 mg at night. I also take saw palmetto, 160 mg twice a day, because my neighbor told me it helps the prostate.
Doctor: Any allergies?
Patient: No, none.
Doctor: Okay. Your vitals today are blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 76, temperature 98.4, and oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Let me examine you. On the rectal exam the prostate is mildly enlarged, smooth, symmetric, and not tender. I don't feel any hard nodules. The belly is soft and there's no tenderness over the bladder. We did a urine dip while you were waiting, and it showed no blood, no white cells, and the nitrite was negative.
Patient: So is it cancer?
Doctor: I can't tell you that from today. An enlarged prostate from age alone can raise the PSA, but a jump from 3.9 to 6.8 deserves a proper work up. So my impression is an elevated PSA with a mildly enlarged prostate, probably benign prostate enlargement causing your night time urination and weak stream, along with high blood pressure that is well controlled. Here is the plan. I'm going to start tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day at bedtime for the urinary symptoms. I want you to stop the saw palmetto, since it won't help and it can muddy things. Keep taking the lisinopril and the atorvastatin. We'll repeat the PSA in six weeks, and no bike riding or ejaculation for two days before the draw. I'm also referring you to urology for an MRI of the prostate. If you get a fever, can't pass urine, or see blood, come back right away.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good. Thank you.
summary: A 68-year-old male came to urgent care after his regular doctor told him his PSA had risen to 6.8 from 3.9 two years earlier. He has had a weak stream and night time urination for about a year, and he denies burning, blood in the urine, fever, bone pain, and weight loss. Vitals were stable, the rectal exam showed a mildly enlarged, smooth, nontender prostate without nodules, and the urine dip was negative for blood, white cells, and nitrite. The impression is elevated PSA with probable benign prostate enlargement and well controlled high blood pressure. Tamsulosin was started, saw palmetto stopped, and lisinopril and atorvastatin continued, with a repeat PSA in six weeks and urology referral for a prostate MRI.

Takes lisinopril 20 mg once a day for blood pressure, atorvastatin 20 mg at night, and saw palmetto 160 mg twice a day. No allergies.

Rectal exam: prostate mildly enlarged, smooth, symmetric, not tender, no hard nodules. Abdomen soft with no tenderness over the bladder. Urine dip showed no blood, no white cells, and negative nitrite. PSA was reported as 6.8, previously 3.9.
soap.assessment: Elevated PSA with a mildly enlarged prostate, probably benign prostate enlargement causing night time urination and weak stream; high blood pressure that is well controlled.
plan: Start tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day at bedtime for the urinary symptoms
Stop saw palmetto
Continue lisinopril and atorvastatin
Repeat the PSA in six weeks, with no bike riding or ejaculation for two days before the draw
Refer to urology for an MRI of the prostate
Return right away for fever, inability to pass urine, or blood in the urine

note:
PSYCH CONSULT, adult ADHD eval. Requested by medicine team, HD#4.
45-year-old male, admitted to med ward w/ EtOH withdrawal, on CIWA protocol, improving.

RFC: pt c/o life-long poor focus, wants "my ADHD meds" started.

HPI:
- c/o inattention since grade school, loses keys/wallet, misses deadlines at work, starts tasks and doesn't finish
- c/o restlessness, interrupts others, impulsive spending
- sx began before age 12 per pt, teachers called him a "daydreamer", repeated detentions; mother (by phone) c/w this
- worse x2 yrs w/ heavier drinking
- denies depressed mood, denies SI, denies HI, denies AH/VH
- denies decreased need for sleep, denies grandiosity
- no prior ADHD dx or stimulant tx
- EtOH: pt first says "6 beers/day". Later, correction, 12 beers/day x5 yrs plus vodka on weekends, after we reviewed the BAL result together. Last drink 4 days ago PTA.

PMH: HTN, T2DM, GERD, hepatic steatosis, MDD (remote)
Meds PTA: lisinopril 10 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BID, omeprazole 20 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, bupropion XL 300 mg daily (outside PCP started 2 mo ago "for focus"). Correction: pharmacy fill hx shows bupropion XL 150 mg daily, pt misremembered dose.
Inpt meds: lorazepam 1 mg q6h PRN CIWA >10, thiamine 100 mg daily, folic acid 1 mg daily, gabapentin 300 mg TID (started by medicine). Metformin held. Medicine increased lisinopril 10 mg to 20 mg daily today for BP.
NKDA.
SH: lives w/ wife and 2 kids, warehouse supervisor, 1 ppd smoker. Denies other drug use. FH father w/ AUD.

Vitals: BP 148/92, HR 98, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA
MSE: appears stated age, mild tremor, cooperative, good eye contact. Speech nl rate/volume. Mood "tired", affect anxious. TP linear. No SI/HI, no AH/VH, no delusions. A&Ox3. Attn impaired: serial 7s w/ errors, WORLD backwards 3/5 (confounded by withdrawal). Insight/judgment fair.
Labs: AST 88, ALT 62, MCV 102, Na 136, K 3.6, Cr 0.9, Plt 142, A1c 7.1, TSH 2.1, BAL on admission 0.28, UDS neg.
ASRS screener 5/6 positive.

Imp:
- adult ADHD, r/o. Hx c/w childhood-onset inattention/impulsivity but dx cannot be made now, confounded by heavy EtOH and withdrawal
- AUD, severe, in early EtOH withdrawal
- MDD, remote, no active depressive sx

Recs:
- NO stimulant now (active EtOH use, withdrawal, BP 148/92)
- d/c bupropion XL 150 mg (lowers seizure threshold in withdrawal)
- cont sertraline 50 mg daily
- cont CIWA, thiamine, folic acid, gabapentin per medicine
- start naltrexone 50 mg daily before d/c, AST 88 is <3x ULN, ok
- repeat formal ADHD eval (DIVA, collateral, school records) after >=4 wks abstinence as outpt; non-stimulant tx preferred if dx confirmed given AUD
- refer addiction med for outpt AUD tx
- psych f/u 4-6 wks, call if SI
summary: A 45-year-old male on the medical ward for alcohol withdrawal was seen by psychiatry for adult ADHD evaluation, reporting lifelong inattention, restlessness, and impulsivity. He drinks about 12 beers daily, takes bupropion XL 150 mg daily from an outside doctor, and has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, GERD, hepatic steatosis, and remote depression. He denies depressed mood, SI, HI, and hallucinations, and his attention was impaired but confounded by withdrawal. ADHD could not be confirmed during heavy drinking and withdrawal, and severe AUD was assessed. Stimulants were deferred, bupropion stopped, sertraline continued, naltrexone planned, and a repeat ADHD evaluation advised after four weeks of abstinence.

note:
Telehealth visit via secure video. Patient is at home with her daughter in the room. Verbal consent for the video visit obtained. 57-year-old female with hidradenitis suppurativa, here for follow-up of a flare.

History: Patient reports painful, draining nodules in the left axilla and both groin folds for about 3 weeks, worse than her usual baseline. Her daughter, who helps with dressing changes every day, adds that the bandages are soaked twice a day now and that her mother has been waking at night because of the pain, although her mother tends to downplay it. Patient rates the pain 7 out of 10. She denies fever, denies chills, denies spreading redness beyond the lesions, and denies new lesions on the buttocks. She smokes about half a pack of cigarettes a day. She has type 2 diabetes. Current medications are metformin 1000 mg BID and clindamycin 1% lotion applied BID to the affected areas, used for 8 weeks with little benefit. She takes ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for pain. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: temperature 98.4 F, BP 132/80, pulse 82 on her home cuff. A1c from her primary care doctor last month was 7.8%. Wound culture from the left axilla at the previous visit grew methicillin-sensitive Staph aureus.

Exam by video, limited, with the daughter holding the tablet: left axilla has 3 tender inflamed nodules and one draining sinus tract with surrounding scarring, no streaking or spreading erythema. Right axilla has old scarring without active lesions. Groin folds seen briefly, with two inflamed nodules on the right and one on the left. Patient is comfortable and speaking in full sentences.

Impression: Hurley stage II hidradenitis suppurativa with an active flare of the left axilla and both groin folds. Type 2 diabetes with suboptimal control. Tobacco use, which worsens the disease.

Plan:
Stop clindamycin lotion since it has not helped.
Start doxycycline 100 mg BID for 12 weeks, taken with food and a full glass of water, with counseling on sun sensitivity.
Continue metformin and ibuprofen as needed.
Daughter instructed on non-adherent absorbent dressings and warm compresses.
Smoking cessation counseling provided and patient will think about nicotine replacement.
Repeat A1c with her primary care doctor in 2 months.
In-person visit in 4 weeks to consider intralesional triamcinolone injection and discuss adalimumab if no improvement.
Return sooner for fever or spreading redness.

note: This is a nephrology consultation dictation on hospital day 2 for a 64-year-old male with chronic kidney disease stage 3b who was admitted with acute kidney injury. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He returned from a three week trip to India ten days ago, correction, nine days ago, and about five days after returning he developed watery diarrhea, up to eight stools a day, with nausea, poor oral intake and decreased urine output. He denies blood in the stool, denies fever, denies flank pain, denies dysuria and denies leg swelling. During the trip he took ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a day for back pain. Baseline creatinine is 1.9 with an eGFR of 36. Home medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID, amlodipine 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. On admission blood pressure was 98/60 and heart rate 108. Today vitals are blood pressure 112/68, heart rate 88, temperature 98.8 Fahrenheit and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam he looks mildly dry with tacky mucous membranes, lungs are clear, the abdomen is soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no costovertebral angle tenderness and no edema. Admission labs show creatinine 2.9, BUN 54, potassium 5.4, bicarbonate 17 and sodium 133. Today creatinine is 2.4 after fluids and potassium is 4.8, correction, 4.9. Lactate is 1.4. Urinalysis is bland with trace protein and no blood, and the urine sodium concentration is low. Renal ultrasound shows normal sized echogenic kidneys with no hydronephrosis. Stool culture and ova and parasites are pending. My impression is acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease stage 3b, prerenal from volume depletion due to infectious diarrhea, worsened by an ACE inhibitor and NSAID exposure. Recommendations are normal saline at 100 mL per hour for 12 hours then reassess, hold lisinopril, hold metformin, and hold amlodipine while his pressure is low, stop ibuprofen and avoid NSAIDs and contrast, continue atorvastatin, renally dose all medications, strict intake and output with daily weights, and a basic metabolic panel every morning. Restart lisinopril only when creatinine returns to baseline. Nephrology will follow daily and he should see us in clinic two weeks after discharge.
summary: A 64-year-old male with chronic kidney disease stage 3b, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension was admitted with acute kidney injury after watery diarrhea following a three week trip to India. He denies blood in the stool, fever, flank pain, dysuria, and leg swelling, and he had taken ibuprofen during the trip. Creatinine rose from a baseline of 1.9 to 2.9 and improved to 2.4 after fluids, with a bland urinalysis and a renal ultrasound without hydronephrosis. The impression is prerenal acute kidney injury from volume depletion due to infectious diarrhea, worsened by an ACE inhibitor and NSAID exposure. Normal saline was recommended, lisinopril, metformin, and amlodipine held, and ibuprofen stopped.

note: Dictating a clinic note on a 94-year-old female seen for urinary incontinence. She has been leaking urine for about eight months, mostly when she feels a sudden strong urge and cannot reach the bathroom in time, and she gets up twice a night to urinate, correction, three times a night. She uses two pads a day. She denies burning with urination, denies blood in the urine, denies fever, denies back pain and denies any falls. Her only chronic problem is hypertension and her only medication is furosemide 20 mg once daily, which she takes around eight in the evening. On exam blood pressure is 138/74 and heart rate is 70. She is alert, answers questions appropriately and walks with a cane. The abdomen is soft and nontender without suprapubic fullness. Urinalysis today shows no white cells, no nitrite and no blood. A bladder scan after she voided showed a post-void residual of 40 mL. My impression is urge urinary incontinence with nocturia, likely made worse by taking her diuretic in the evening, with no sign of infection or retention. Plan is to move the furosemide to the morning, limit fluids and caffeine after dinner, timed voiding every two to three hours while awake, a bedside commode at night, and no bladder-calming anticholinergic medication given her age and the risk of confusion. Recheck in six weeks.

She denies burning with urination, blood in the urine, fever, back pain, and falls, and she takes only furosemide 20 mg once daily in the evening. Blood pressure was 138/74, the urinalysis was clean, and the post-void residual was 40 mL. The impression is urge urinary incontinence with nocturia, likely worsened by evening diuretic timing, without infection or retention. The furosemide will be moved to the morning, with fluid and caffeine limits, timed voiding, a bedside commode, avoidance of anticholinergic medication, and recheck in six weeks.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I am using a professional Spanish interpreter on the video line, so please use short sentences and we will pause for the interpreter. I have you down as an 88-year-old male here about problems passing urine. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. I have trouble to start the urine, the stream is weak, and I go all the time. At night I get up four times.
Doctor: How long has this been going on?
Patient: More than two years, but now it is worse. I feel like the bladder never empties.
Doctor: Any burning, blood in the urine, or fever?
Patient: No burning. No blood. No fever.
Doctor: Have there been times when you could not pass urine at all?
Patient: No, never completely stopped.
Doctor: Have you fallen recently?
Patient: Not fallen, but when I stand up fast at night I get dizzy and I have to hold the wall.
Doctor: I see. Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: I take tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day, lisinopril 10 mg once a day, amlodipine 10 mg once a day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, aspirin 81 mg once a day, and a pill for the bladder, oxybutynin, 10 mg twice a day.
Doctor: Let me check, because the pharmacy list in your chart says oxybutynin 5 mg twice a day. Can you look at the bottle?
Patient: Ah, yes, the bottle says 5 mg. I said it wrong. It is 5 mg twice a day.
Doctor: Thank you, that is helpful. So oxybutynin is 5 mg twice a day. Any allergies?
Patient: No allergies.
Doctor: And who helps you at home?
Patient: I live alone since my wife died. My daughter lives in another state and calls on Sundays. A neighbor checks on me sometimes, but not every day. I take the pills out of the bottles by myself. I do not have a pill box.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. We will work on that. Now your vitals. Lying down your blood pressure is 150/82 with a heart rate of 72. After standing for three minutes it falls to 122/70, and you felt dizzy, right?
Patient: Yes, very dizzy.
Doctor: On exam, your belly is soft and I can feel fullness above the pubic bone, so the bladder is not emptying well. On the rectal exam, the prostate is large, about 60 grams by feel, smooth and firm, with no hard nodules. Your IPSS score today is 24, which is severe. The bladder scan after you urinated shows 180 mL left behind. Your urine test today had no blood and no infection. The blood tests from last week show creatinine 1.4 and a PSA of 2.9. The ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder showed no swelling of the kidneys, and the prostate measured about 62 grams.
Patient: Is it cancer?
Doctor: The PSA is not high for a man your age with a large prostate, and the rectal exam did not feel suspicious. My impression is benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms and incomplete bladder emptying. The oxybutynin is probably making it worse, and the tamsulosin together with the amlodipine is causing low blood pressure on standing. You also have hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease, which your primary doctor manages.
Patient: What do we do?
Doctor: Here is the plan. Stop the oxybutynin, because it can trap urine in the bladder. Start finasteride 5 mg once a day to shrink the prostate slowly, and it can take about six months. Keep the tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day, but take it after dinner. Lower the amlodipine from 10 mg to 5 mg once a day because of the dizziness when you stand, and I will send a note to your primary doctor. Keep the lisinopril, metformin, and aspirin the same. Because your creatinine is 1.4, your primary doctor will watch the metformin. We will repeat the bladder scan and the standing blood pressure in four weeks. Because you live alone, I am asking our social worker to call you with an interpreter, to arrange a home health nurse to fill a weekly pill box, and to ask about a medical alert button. Stand up slowly, sit on the edge of the bed for one minute first, keep a night light on, and use a urinal at the bedside. If you cannot pass urine at all, or you have a fever, or you fall, go to the emergency room.
Patient: I understand. Thank you, doctor.
summary: An 88-year-old male with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease was seen through a professional interpreter for worsening weak stream, frequent urination, nocturia four times nightly, and incomplete emptying. He lives alone with limited support, felt dizzy on standing with blood pressure dropping from 150/82 to 122/70, and had a post-void residual of 180 mL, an IPSS of 24, PSA 2.9, and creatinine 1.4. The impression is benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms, worsened by oxybutynin and low blood pressure on standing. Oxybutynin was stopped, finasteride started, amlodipine reduced to 5 mg, and social work and home health arranged.

soap.subjective: 88-year-old male seen with a professional Spanish interpreter for more than two years of worsening trouble starting urine, weak stream, frequent urination, getting up four times at night, and a feeling that the bladder never empties. He denies burning, blood in the urine, fever, and complete inability to pass urine. He has dizziness on standing at night but has not fallen. Takes tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day, lisinopril 10 mg once a day, amlodipine 10 mg once a day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, aspirin 81 mg once a day, and oxybutynin 5 mg twice a day (he first said 10 mg; the bottle and pharmacy list confirmed 5 mg). soap.objective: Lying blood pressure 150/82 with heart rate 72; after standing three minutes blood pressure 122/70 with dizziness. Abdomen soft with fullness above the pubic bone. Rectal exam: prostate large, about 60 grams by feel, smooth and firm, no hard nodules. IPSS score 24. Bladder scan after voiding 180 mL. Urine test with no blood and no infection. Creatinine 1.4 and PSA 2.9 from last week. Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder with no swelling of the kidneys and prostate about 62 grams.
soap.assessment: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms and incomplete bladder emptying, likely worsened by oxybutynin. Low blood pressure on standing from tamsulosin together with amlodipine. Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease managed by his primary doctor.
plan: Stop oxybutynin because it can trap urine in the bladder
Start finasteride 5 mg once a day; benefit may take about six months
Continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day, taken after dinner
Reduce amlodipine from 10 mg to 5 mg once a day because of dizziness on standing, and send a note to his primary doctor

Repeat the bladder scan and standing blood pressure in four weeks
Social worker to call with an interpreter, arrange a home health nurse to fill a weekly pill box, and ask about a medical alert button
Stand up slowly, sit on the edge of the bed for one minute first, use a night light and a bedside urinal
Go to the emergency room if unable to pass urine at all, fever, or a fall

procedures: ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder

note:
Visit type: telephone only, no video. Patient identified with two identifiers, agreed to a phone visit, and was at home. 57-year-old male referred to pulmonology for chronic cough.

History: Cough for about 4 months, dry and tickling, worse when lying down at night and when talking, with no sputum. Patient is quite anxious and asked many questions during the call, including whether this could be lung cancer because his father died of it, whether the cough is contagious, and whether he needs a CT scan. He denies fever, denies hemoptysis, denies shortness of breath, denies wheezing, denies night sweats, and denies weight loss. He reports occasional heartburn. Former smoker, about 10 pack-years, quit 20 years ago. Medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily, started about 5 months ago for hypertension, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He tried over-the-counter dextromethorphan syrup with no benefit. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: pulse oximeter 98% on room air, BP 134/84, heart rate 78.
Exam: none by phone. He speaks in full sentences with no audible wheeze or stridor and coughed twice during the 15 minute call.
Results reviewed: chest x-ray 2 weeks ago was clear with no mass or infiltrate. Spirometry last week was normal.

Impression: Chronic cough, most likely ACE inhibitor-induced cough since it began after starting lisinopril, with possible contribution from reflux. Hypertension, controlled at home. His anxiety about the cough improved after discussion.

Plan:
Stop lisinopril today.
Start losartan 50 mg daily for blood pressure.
Start omeprazole 20 mg daily before breakfast for 8 weeks and raise the head of the bed.
Dextromethorphan is not helping, so he can stop it.
Explained that the cough usually improves within 1 to 4 weeks after stopping an ACE inhibitor but can take up to 3 months. Answered his questions at length: the normal chest x-ray and spirometry are reassuring, the cough is not contagious, and a CT scan is not needed unless the cough persists 8 weeks after stopping lisinopril or red flags develop. He verbalized understanding and sounded calmer by the end of the call.
BMP in 2 weeks to check potassium and creatinine after starting losartan.
Keep a home BP log. Phone follow-up in 4 weeks.
Call or go to the ED for coughing up blood, shortness of breath, fever, or weight loss.

Doctor: Hi, thanks for bringing her in. So this is a 1-year-old female here for a skin rash, is that right?
Family member: Yes. Her eczema has gotten a lot worse over the last two weeks. She is scratching her cheeks and her arms and legs, and she is fussy at night because of the itching.
Doctor: How long has she had the eczema?
Family member: Since she was about four months old. It comes and goes, but this is the worst it has been.
Doctor: What have you been using on it?
Family member: Hydrocortisone 1% ointment twice a day, and I put petroleum jelly on after her bath.
Doctor: Is it helping?
Family member: It helps on her face, but the patches on her body don't get better.
Doctor: Any fever?
Family member: No fever.
Doctor: Any oozing, crusting, or yellow scabs?
Family member: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any vomiting, diarrhea, hives, or trouble breathing after she eats?
Family member: No. But her cheeks look redder after she eats egg, so I wonder about an allergy.
Doctor: Okay. Any medicine allergies?
Family member: None.
Doctor: Let me examine her. Her weight is 9.8 kilograms, temperature 98.9, heart rate 120, and respiratory rate 28. On her skin she has dry, red, scaly patches on both cheeks, on the trunk, and in the creases of the elbows and knees. There are scratch marks, but no oozing, no crusting, and no pustules. Her diaper area is spared. Her lungs are clear. The blood test we sent at the last visit came back with an egg white specific IgE of 1.2 kU/L, which is a low positive. That means she is sensitized to egg, but it does not prove she is truly allergic.
Family member: So should I stop giving her egg?
Doctor: Please hold off on egg for now, until the allergist sees her. My impression is a flare of atopic dermatitis, and she is sensitized to egg. For the body patches, start triamcinolone 0.025% ointment twice a day for 7 days, and keep it off her face and diaper area. Continue hydrocortisone 1% ointment twice a day on the face. Keep using the petroleum jelly at least twice a day, with short lukewarm baths and fragrance-free soap. I will refer her to pediatric allergy. We will recheck in two weeks, and come back sooner if she gets a fever, oozing, or crusting.
Family member: Okay, thank you.

Exam showed dry, red, scaly patches on the cheeks, trunk, and elbow and knee creases with scratch marks and no infection, and a prior egg white specific IgE was a low positive at 1.2 kU/L. The impression is an atopic dermatitis flare with sensitization to egg. Triamcinolone 0.025% ointment was started for the body patches for 7 days, hydrocortisone 1% continued on the face, egg avoided pending pediatric allergy referral, and recheck set for two weeks.

The patient is a 41-year-old female seen in the orthopedic clinic for low back pain that goes down the left leg for about 6 weeks. She describes the pain as "like electricity" that starts in the buttock and travels down the back of the thigh to the outside of the calf and the top of the foot. It is worse with sitting, coughing, and bending, and better when she lies on her side. She denies fever, weight loss, loss of bowel or bladder control, numbness in the groin, and any recent injury. She works in a hotel laundry and lifts heavy loads all day.

She has limited health literacy. She did not know the names of her medicines and brought all of her bottles, and we reviewed each bottle together. She reports leaving school after the sixth grade and relies on pictures and a family member to read labels. I used plain language, short sentences, and teach-back throughout the visit. She has hypertension and takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. For the pain she has been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen 200 mg, two tablets about three times a day, with only partial relief. She has no known drug allergies.

On examination blood pressure was 138/86 and heart rate 78. Gait is normal. There is tenderness over the left lower lumbar paraspinal muscles. The straight leg raise is positive on the left at about 40 degrees and reproduces the leg pain. Great toe extension strength is 4/5 on the left and 5/5 on the right, and sensation is decreased over the top of the left foot. Knee and ankle reflexes are symmetric, and there is no saddle numbness. Lumbar spine x-rays show mild disc space narrowing at L4-L5 without fracture or slippage.

My impression is left L5 lumbar radiculopathy, most likely from a disc herniation at L4-L5, with hypertension that is stable. I ordered an MRI of the lumbar spine. I stopped the ibuprofen and started naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food for 2 weeks, and asked her to check her blood pressure at the pharmacy because naproxen can raise it. I also started gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime, which may be increased at follow-up. I referred her to physical therapy and gave her a work note for light duty with no heavy lifting. Using teach-back, she correctly named the new pills by their pictures on the handout and explained when to take them. She was given a picture-based handout and a pill organizer. She should go to the emergency room right away if she develops leg weakness that is getting worse, numbness in the groin, or trouble controlling urine or stool. Follow-up in 4 weeks to review the MRI.

She denies fever, weight loss, bowel or bladder control loss, groin numbness, and recent injury. Exam showed a positive left straight leg raise, 4/5 left great toe extension, and decreased sensation over the top of the left foot, and lumbar x-rays showed mild disc space narrowing at L4-L5. The impression is left L5 lumbar radiculopathy, most likely from a disc herniation, with stable hypertension. Ibuprofen was stopped, naproxen and gabapentin started, an MRI and physical therapy ordered, and teach-back with a picture-based handout used for instructions.

The patient is a 55-year-old female seen in the gastroenterology clinic to discuss colorectal cancer screening. She has never had a colonoscopy or any stool-based screening test. She denies rectal bleeding, black stools, change in bowel habits, abdominal pain, and unintentional weight loss. She has no family history of colon cancer, colon polyps, or inflammatory bowel disease. Her medical history includes hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease. She is postmenopausal and had a hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 8 years ago for fibroids, so pregnancy is not a consideration when choosing her bowel preparation or sedation. Current medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, which she started on her own last year for low energy. She has no known drug allergies.

Blood pressure today is 126/78 and heart rate is 70. The abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended with no masses and normal bowel sounds. Laboratory results from last month show hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL and ferritin 62 ng/mL, so there is no evidence of iron deficiency anemia.

I reviewed the three reasonable options for an average-risk patient: colonoscopy every 10 years, an annual stool immunochemical test, or a multitarget stool DNA test every 3 years. I explained that a positive stool test would still require a colonoscopy. After discussing the benefits and risks, including the small risks of bleeding and perforation with colonoscopy and the need for a driver, she chose to proceed with colonoscopy. I reviewed the split-dose bowel preparation with polyethylene glycol, 4 liters total, with the first 2 liters the evening before and the second 2 liters 5 hours before the procedure, and a clear liquid diet the day before. She repeated the instructions back accurately.

Impression is an average-risk patient due for first screening colonoscopy, along with hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease that are both stable. Plan is to schedule a screening colonoscopy under monitored sedation. Start the split-dose polyethylene glycol preparation as described. Stop ferrous sulfate 7 days before the procedure so it does not darken the stool and limit visualization. Continue amlodipine, including the morning of the procedure with a sip of water, and continue omeprazole. She will arrange a driver. Return after colonoscopy to review results and set the next screening interval.

She denies rectal bleeding, black stools, change in bowel habits, abdominal pain, and weight loss, has no family history of colorectal disease, and had a hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, so pregnancy is not a prescribing concern. Exam was benign and hemoglobin 13.4 and ferritin 62 were normal. After reviewing colonoscopy and stool-based options, she chose a screening colonoscopy. A split-dose polyethylene glycol preparation was started, ferrous sulfate is to be stopped 7 days beforehand, and amlodipine and omeprazole continue.

Doctor: Hello, I have you down as a 25-year-old female here for trouble swallowing. Tell me about it.
Patient: Over the last two years food has started to get stuck, mostly when I eat meat, bread, or rice. It has gotten worse over the last six months. Now I cut everything into tiny pieces and drink a lot of water with every bite.
Doctor: Where does it get stuck?
Patient: Right in the middle of my chest, behind the breastbone.
Doctor: Has it ever stuck completely?
Patient: Yes, once about two months ago at a restaurant with chicken. I couldn't swallow even my saliva, and after about twenty minutes I threw it up and it passed.
Doctor: Do liquids go down okay?
Patient: Yes, liquids are fine.
Doctor: Any pain when you swallow?
Patient: No pain when swallowing, just the stuck feeling. I do get heartburn a couple of times a week.
Doctor: Any weight loss, vomiting blood, or black stools?
Patient: No, my weight is the same, no blood, and my stools are normal.
Doctor: What other health problems do you have?
Patient: I have had asthma and eczema since I was a kid, and seasonal allergies.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Omeprazole 20 mg once a day, over the counter, for the heartburn, but it hasn't really helped. An albuterol inhaler when I need it, and cetirizine 10 mg every day during the spring.
Doctor: Any drug allergies?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure today is 112/68, heart rate 72, and your weight is stable compared with last visit. Your mouth and throat look normal, your neck has no masses, your lungs are clear, and your belly is soft and not tender. The blood work you had last week showed a hemoglobin of 13.1 and a negative tissue transglutaminase antibody, so no sign of anemia or celiac disease.
Patient: So what do you think is going on?
Doctor: You are young, you have asthma, eczema, and allergies, and you have food sticking with one episode where it was fully stuck. My main concern is eosinophilic esophagitis, which is an allergic type of inflammation in the esophagus. We can't diagnose it from symptoms alone. I would like to do an upper endoscopy, an EGD, with biopsies of the esophagus. In the meantime, I am going to increase your omeprazole from 20 mg once a day to 40 mg twice a day, before breakfast and dinner, for 8 weeks. Keep the albuterol and cetirizine as you have been using them. Please chew food very well, cut it into small pieces, and avoid big pieces of dry meat or bread until the endoscopy. If food gets stuck and you can't swallow your saliva, go to the emergency room. We will schedule a follow-up visit after the EGD to go over the biopsy results.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.
summary: A 25-year-old female with asthma, eczema, and seasonal allergies reported two years of progressive trouble swallowing solids, worse over the last six months, with one episode two months ago when chicken stuck completely. She also has heartburn a couple of times a week that over-the-counter omeprazole has not helped, and she denies pain when swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, and black stools. Vitals and exam were unremarkable, with hemoglobin 13.1 and a negative tissue transglutaminase antibody. The main concern is eosinophilic esophagitis. An upper endoscopy with biopsies was planned, omeprazole was increased from 20 mg once a day to 40 mg twice a day for 8 weeks, and eating precautions and emergency instructions were given.

Liquids are fine. Heartburn a couple of times a week. Denies pain when swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, and black stools. Has had asthma and eczema since childhood and seasonal allergies. Takes omeprazole 20 mg once a day over the counter without much help, an albuterol inhaler when needed, and cetirizine 10 mg every day in spring. No drug allergies.

Go to the emergency room if food gets stuck and she cannot swallow her saliva

Doctor: Hi there. I see a 7-year-old male here for coughing and wheezing. What has been going on?
Family member: He caught a cold three days ago, and last night the cough got much worse and I could hear him wheezing. He has been breathing fast and says his chest feels tight.
Doctor: Has he had a fever?
Family member: No fever. And no vomiting.
Doctor: He has asthma, right?
Family member: Yes, since he was four. He has an albuterol inhaler. I gave him 2 puffs last night and again this morning, and it only helped a little.
Doctor: Any medicine allergies?
Family member: None.
Doctor: Can you tell me how you feel?
Patient: My chest feels tight and I get tired when I walk fast.
Doctor: Okay. Let me listen. His temperature is 98.6, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 26, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. He talks in full sentences, there are no retractions, and I hear mild wheezing at the end of each breath in both lungs with good air movement.
Family member: Is it serious?
Doctor: It is a mild asthma exacerbation set off by the cold. Let's start prednisone 20 mg once a day for 5 days to calm the inflammation. Keep using the albuterol, 2 puffs every 4 hours while he is awake for the next two days with the spacer, and then only as needed. Please keep him home from school until he is breathing comfortably. Go to the emergency room if he can't speak in full sentences, his ribs pull in when he breathes, his lips look blue, or the albuterol doesn't last four hours. I'd like to see him back in a week.
Family member: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 7-year-old male with asthma had three days of cold symptoms followed by worse cough, wheezing, fast breathing, and chest tightness that only partly improved with albuterol. He has no fever or vomiting. Exam showed temperature 98.6, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 96 percent, full sentences, no retractions, and mild end-expiratory wheezing in both lungs. The impression is a mild asthma exacerbation triggered by the cold. Prednisone 20 mg once a day for 5 days was started, albuterol 2 puffs every 4 hours with a spacer for two days then as needed, with school absence, return precautions, and recheck in a week.

soap.subjective: 7-year-old male with asthma since age four who caught a cold three days ago, with a much worse cough and audible wheezing last night, fast breathing, and chest tightness. Albuterol 2 puffs last night and this morning helped only a little. Gets tired when walking fast. Denies fever and vomiting. No medicine allergies.
soap.objective: Temperature 98.6, heart rate 100, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Talks in full sentences, no retractions, mild wheezing at the end of each breath in both lungs with good air movement.
soap.assessment: Mild asthma exacerbation set off by a cold.

Albuterol 2 puffs every 4 hours while awake for the next two days with a spacer, then only as needed
Keep him home from school until breathing comfortably
Go to the emergency room for inability to speak in full sentences, ribs pulling in, blue lips, or albuterol not lasting four hours
Return visit in a week

note:
Visit modality: synchronous video visit. Patient is at home and her mother is in the room and joins the call to help with parts of the history because the patient is tired. Verbal consent for telehealth obtained. 32-year-old female with burning with urination and urinary frequency.

HPI: Patient reports burning with urination and needing to urinate about every hour, and she first says this has been going on for 5 days. Her mother clarifies that it actually started 3 days ago, right after the patient got home from a two week trip to Mexico, and the patient agrees. She also has urgency and mild suprapubic pressure. She denies fever, denies chills, denies flank pain, denies vomiting, denies vaginal discharge, and denies visible blood in the urine. She had loose stools during the trip that resolved before she flew home, with no current diarrhea, and she drank mostly bottled water while traveling. She has had no previous urinary tract infections in the past year and no history of kidney stones. She took over-the-counter phenazopyridine 200 mg three times a day for 2 days with partial relief.

PMH: hypothyroidism, asthma, migraine.
Medications: levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, albuterol inhaler as needed, sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine, and the phenazopyridine as above.
Allergies: sulfa antibiotics, which cause hives.
Pregnancy: home urine pregnancy test this morning was negative.

Home measurements: temperature 98.7 F, BP 118/72, heart rate 84 on her home cuff. Her mother held the camera while the patient read a home urine dipstick, which was positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite with trace blood. TSH last week from her primary care doctor was 6.8, with a normal free T4 of 0.9.

Exam by video, limited: appears tired but not toxic, speaking in full sentences with no respiratory distress. She points to mild tenderness above the pubic bone when she presses there and no tenderness over either flank.

Impression: Uncomplicated acute cystitis (urinary tract infection) in a recent traveler. Hypothyroidism with elevated TSH, under-replaced. Asthma and migraine stable.

Plan:
Start nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID for 5 days with food. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole avoided because of her sulfa allergy.
Urine culture at the lab today before the first dose because of recent travel and the risk of a resistant organism.
Stop phenazopyridine because it can interfere with urine tests and should not be used longer than 2 days.
Increase levothyroxine from 75 mcg to 88 mcg daily on an empty stomach, with repeat TSH in 6 to 8 weeks.
Continue albuterol and sumatriptan as needed.
Drink plenty of fluids.
Phone call in 3 days with the culture result. Seek care for fever, flank pain, vomiting, or no improvement within 48 hours.

She denies fever, chills, flank pain, vomiting, vaginal discharge, visible blood, and diarrhea, has a sulfa allergy, and her home pregnancy test was negative. Home dipstick was positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite, and her recent TSH was 6.8. The impression is uncomplicated acute cystitis in a recent traveler and under-replaced hypothyroidism. Nitrofurantoin was started, a urine culture ordered, phenazopyridine stopped, and levothyroxine increased from 75 to 88 mcg daily.

note: Dictation for a 78-year-old female seen in the outpatient clinic for gradual hearing loss. She reports about three years, correction, about four years of slowly worsening hearing in both ears, trouble following conversation in restaurants and when people speak from another room, and she keeps the television volume high. She has mild ringing in both ears. She denies ear pain, denies ear drainage, denies dizziness, and denies any sudden change in her hearing. Her only chronic condition is open-angle glaucoma, for which she uses latanoprost 0.005% eye drops, one drop in each eye at bedtime. On examination the ear canals are clear without wax and the eardrums are intact and normal on both sides. With tuning fork testing the Weber is midline and Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone conduction in both ears. The audiogram today shows a symmetric moderate high frequency sensorineural hearing loss in both ears, with word recognition 80 percent on the right and 76 percent on the left. For the eyes, visual acuity is 20/40 in each eye with her glasses and eye pressure is 16 in both eyes, both unchanged from her last eye visit. Impression is age-related hearing loss and stable open-angle glaucoma. Plan is referral to audiology for hearing aid fitting, continue latanoprost eye drops nightly, avoid loud noise exposure, repeat audiogram in one year, and routine eye follow up in six months.

Doctor: Good morning. It's nice to see you again. I have you down as a 69-year-old male here for your Parkinson's disease follow-up. How have things been since the last visit?
Patient: Mostly okay, but the pills don't seem to last as long. About three hours after my morning dose, and again in the afternoon, I get slow and stiff and my tremor comes back before the next dose.
Doctor: What are you taking right now?
Patient: Carbidopa-levodopa 25/100, one tablet three times a day, and rasagiline 1 mg every morning.
Doctor: Any falls?
Patient: No falls.
Doctor: Any hallucinations, or seeing things that aren't there?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any dizziness when you stand up?
Patient: No dizziness.
Doctor: How about trouble swallowing or choking?
Patient: No trouble swallowing.
Doctor: How is your sleep? Any acting out your dreams?
Patient: Sleep is okay. No acting out dreams.
Doctor: And your bowels?
Patient: Constipated. I go only every three or four days, hard stools, and I strain. It has been worse this past year.
Doctor: Okay. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Let me check you. Sitting blood pressure is 130/80 with a heart rate of 68, and standing it is 124/76, so no significant drop. You have a mild resting tremor in the right hand, mild slowness with finger tapping, and cogwheel rigidity in the right arm. Your walk is a little slow with less arm swing on the right, and it takes you three steps to turn. The pull test is stable, you recovered on your own. Your MoCA score today was 27 out of 30, which is normal.
Patient: Good. Is the Parkinson's getting worse?
Doctor: Your exam is stable, and what you describe is the medicine wearing off between doses, which is common. My impression is Parkinson's disease with end-of-dose wearing off, and constipation that is most likely from the Parkinson's. Here is the plan. I'm going to increase your carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 from three times a day to four times a day, spaced about every four hours while you are awake, ideally 30 minutes before meals. Continue the rasagiline 1 mg every morning. For the constipation, start polyethylene glycol 17 grams once a day in a glass of water, and drink more fluids, eat more fiber, and walk daily. I'll also send you to physical therapy for gait and balance. Let's see you back in three months, and call sooner if you have falls or hallucinations.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 69-year-old male with Parkinson's disease returned for follow-up reporting that his medication wears off about three hours after the morning dose and again in the afternoon, bringing back slowness, stiffness, and tremor, along with worsening constipation. He denies falls, hallucinations, dizziness on standing, trouble swallowing, and acting out dreams. Sitting and standing blood pressures showed no significant drop, exam showed a mild right-sided resting tremor, bradykinesia, and cogwheel rigidity, and his MoCA was 27 out of 30. The impression is Parkinson's disease with end-of-dose wearing off and constipation. Carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 was increased from three to four times a day, rasagiline continued, polyethylene glycol started, and physical therapy and a three month return arranged.
